# Cloud Compute and Remote Servers {#sec-cloud}

A doctoral student submitted a simulation study to the university
cluster as 200 array tasks and went home. By morning the queue was
empty and the results directory held 169 files: 31 tasks had
exceeded the default memory request and been killed, and the
scheduler had recorded the fact in a log nobody opened. The
summary script averaged the files it found, and the power table in
the draft reported the planned number of replicates for every
scenario, including the largest trials, where the losses were
concentrated. Running out of memory is ordinary; what made this
failure expensive was that it was silent. This chapter is about
running work on someone else's computer, a shared cluster or a
rented cloud machine, without losing the job, the data
governance, or the budget.

## Which resource ran out {#sec-cloud-shortage}

Some analyses outgrow a laptop: multi-core simulations,
genome-scale pipelines, multi-hour model fits. Whether to 'move to
the cloud' is a procurement question, and it is never the useful
one. The useful question is which specific resource has run out.
Wall-clock time, memory, and the availability of your own machine
are three different shortages with three different remedies, and
an analyst who has named the shortage correctly usually finds
that the cheapest adequate remedy is not the public cloud.
@fig-compute-tier puts the tiers in the order a working academic
biostatistician should try them.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-compute-tier
%%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart asking what resource you have run
%%|   out of. Interactive work stays on the laptop. Running out of
%%|   wall-clock time on a parallel job, or out of memory, routes to
%%|   a question about university HPC availability: if available,
%%|   SLURM with Apptainer; if not, or if the queue is too slow, the
%%|   public cloud. Needing specialized hardware such as a GPU or
%%|   very large memory routes directly to the public cloud."
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a compute tier. The laptop is the default and
%%|   the right place for anything interactive. A university cluster
%%|   is usually free and should be tried before a paid cloud. The
%%|   public cloud earns its cost when the cluster is unavailable,
%%|   the queue is too slow, or the job needs hardware the cluster
%%|   does not have."
flowchart TD
  A{"What have you<br/>run out of?"}
  A -->|"nothing, it is<br/>interactive work"| L["Laptop<br/><i>always the default</i>"]
  A -->|"wall-clock time,<br/>job is parallel"| Q{"University HPC<br/>available?"}
  A -->|"memory"| Q
  A -->|"specialized hardware<br/>GPU, very large RAM"| C["Public cloud<br/><i>spot for fault-tolerant work</i>"]
  Q -->|"yes"| H["SLURM plus Apptainer<br/><i>free, queued, no Docker</i>"]
  Q -->|"no, or queue<br/>too slow"| C
```

The flowchart's abbreviations: HPC is high-performance computing,
a university's shared cluster; SLURM is its most common job
scheduler; RAM is random-access memory; and a GPU is a graphics
processing unit. The three shortages differ in kind, not only in
degree:

| Shortage | Typical job | What relieves it | What you are buying |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wall-clock time, parallel work | Ten thousand independent simulation replicates, a bootstrap, a permutation test | More cores | Speed, but less than in proportion to the cores |
| Memory | A genome-scale fit needing 128 GB on a 16 GB laptop | A node or instance with more RAM | Feasibility: the job did not run slowly, it did not run |
| Your own machine | A 24-hour Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) run you would rather not babysit | Any remote machine | A laptop you can close and take home |

: Three shortages and their remedies. {#tbl-cloud-shortages}

Be careful with the arithmetic of the first row, because the naive
version oversells the result. Doubling the cores does not halve
the time: the serial part of the job does not speed up at all, and
the coordination overhead grows with the core count. A simulation
that uses 4 cores does not benefit from a 32-core machine. The
second row differs from the first in kind. On a large-memory
machine the wall-clock time may be no better than the laptop's
would have been had the laptop been able to run the job at all,
and the distinction matters when you justify the cost.

Remote compute is the wrong answer in three cases, and they share
a cause: the round trip to a machine that is not in front of you.
*Interactive exploration* over SSH is laggy, and
exploration is exactly the phase in which you issue many small
commands and look at each result. Anything *latency-sensitive*, a
Shiny app under active debugging above all, is worse for the same
reason. And a *short analysis* is not worth provisioning at any
speed, because thirty seconds of computation is dwarfed by the
minutes of setup, transfer, and teardown around it.

### Profile before you parallelize

Moving a slow job to a bigger machine is tempting because it
needs no code changes, and it is often the wrong first move: a
cloud instance with sixteen cores multiplies a slow step by
sixteen rather than fixing it, and the bill arrives either way.
The bottleneck is frequently not where intuition places it; a
single `data.frame` operation inside a loop, or a function called
once per row instead of once per vector, can dominate a run that
looks, from the outside, like 'the model fit is slow'. Two tools
answer the question before you provision anything.
`profvis::profvis()` records where a script spends its time at the
line level and renders an interactive flame graph; `bench::mark()`
microbenchmarks a small number of candidate expressions against
each other, with memory allocation alongside timing, which a plain
`system.time()` comparison omits.

```r
library(profvis)
library(bench)
# profvis(sim_task(1, reps = 500))         # line-level profile
# bench::mark(loop_version(), vector_version())
```

Both packages are not installed in this book's environment, so the
block above is display-only; install them with `pak::pak()` to run
it yourself. The habit, not the specific tool, is what matters:
profile on a small, fast case on the laptop, fix what the profile
names, and only then decide whether the fixed version still needs
more cores, more memory, or more machines than the laptop has.

### Exercises

1. For each job, name the shortage in @tbl-cloud-shortages and the
   first tier in @fig-compute-tier you would try. (a) A mixed
   model that fails on your laptop with `cannot allocate vector of
   size 24.0 Gb`. (b) A 2,000-replicate simulation of a trial
   design, each replicate taking 40 seconds. (c) Tuning the
   colors of a figure. (d) A one-chain MCMC fit that runs for 30
   hours and uses one core.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Memory: the error is R failing to allocate, not running
slowly. Try a large-memory node on the university cluster; the
public cloud if none exists. (b) Wall-clock time on parallel
work: 2,000 times 40 seconds is about 22 hours serially, and the
replicates are independent, so a cluster job array
(@sec-cloud-hpc) is the natural fit. (c) None: interactive work
stays on the laptop. (d) Your own machine: the job uses one core,
so more cores do not help, but any remote machine frees the
laptop; a cluster batch job is the cheapest.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague proposes moving a 128 GB genomic fit
from a 16 GB laptop to a 64-core cloud instance with 64 GB of
memory 'because it has many more cores'. What is wrong with the
plan?

**Answer.** The shortage is memory, not cores, and 64 GB is still
less than the job needs, so it will fail on the new machine just
as it failed on the laptop, now at an hourly rate. Name the
shortage first: the job needs a machine with more than 128 GB of
memory, and the core count is nearly irrelevant to whether it
runs.
:::

## Batch jobs on a cluster {#sec-cloud-hpc}

For most academic work the first stop is the university cluster:
usually free to affiliated researchers, with R and the common
scientific libraries already installed. The trade-offs are the
queue, the shared environment, and a way of working, batch
submission, that differs from the laptop's.

### Login nodes, compute nodes, and the scheduler

You SSH into a *login node*, which is shared by everyone on the
cluster and is for editing files and submitting jobs, not for
computing. The work runs on *compute nodes*, which a scheduler
allocates. The most common scheduler is SLURM, originally the
Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management
[@yoo2003slurm].[^slurm-name] You describe the job (cores, memory,
time limit) in a batch script; SLURM queues it, runs it when the
resources are free, and kills it if it exceeds what it asked for.

[^slurm-name]: The project now writes its name 'Slurm' and calls
    it a workload manager; the book keeps the capitals most
    cluster documentation still uses.

Most clusters do not permit Docker, for a good reason: the Docker
daemon runs as root, and a shared multi-user cluster cannot grant
every user root. The standard substitute is [**Apptainer**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-apptainer) (formerly
Singularity), a container runtime that runs unprivileged and can
build its image directly from your Docker image
[@kurtzer2017singularity]. The reproducibility argument of
@sec-docker survives the move intact: the image is the same image,
and only the runtime changes.

### A minimal batch script

The script below runs one R script inside the project's image. It
is display-only, like every SLURM and cloud command in this
chapter, because it needs a cluster account.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hfhome-fit
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out

set -euo pipefail
apptainer exec analysis.sif Rscript analysis/scripts/fit.R
```

Convert the image once on the cluster, create the log directory,
and submit (display-only):

```bash
apptainer pull analysis.sif docker://ghcr.io/you/analysis:v1.0
mkdir -p logs
sbatch fit.sbatch                    # prints: Submitted batch job <id>
squeue -u "$USER"                    # pending (PD) or running (R)
```

Each `#SBATCH` line is a request, and each request is a way for
the job to fail:

| Directive | Requests | If it is too small or missing |
|---|---|---|
| `--cpus-per-task` | Cores for one task | Parallel code runs on one core, slowly, without an error |
| `--mem` | Memory per node | The job is killed, and `sacct` reports `OUT_OF_MEMORY` |
| `--time` | Wall-clock limit (hours:minutes:seconds) | The job is killed at the limit, and `sacct` reports `TIMEOUT` |
| `--output` | Log file; `%x` is the job name, `%j` the job ID | SLURM does not create the directory; with no `logs/`, the job fails and leaves no log |

: The `#SBATCH` requests that matter most. Cluster defaults vary;
your cluster's documentation gives them. {#tbl-cloud-sbatch}

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Ask the scheduler how the job ended, rather than reading the log
and assuming (display-only):

```bash
sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ReqMem
```

A clean run shows `COMPLETED` and exit code `0:0` on every line.
`MaxRSS`, the peak memory the job used, should sit comfortably
below `ReqMem`; if it is close, the next run with more data will
be killed. Request about a third more than the peak you observed.
:::

### A simulation study as a job array

A simulation study is the cluster's natural workload: many
independent replicates, each small. A *job array* submits one
script many times, and each copy, a *task*, reads its own index
from `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID`. The array below runs 40 tasks, at most
10 at a time (display-only):

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hfhome-power
#SBATCH --array=1-40%10
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=2G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out

set -euo pipefail
apptainer exec analysis.sif \
  Rscript analysis/scripts/sim_task.R "$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID"
```

`%A` is the array's job ID and `%a` the task index, so each task
writes its own log. The R side is a function of the task index.
The simulation below estimates the power of the HF-HOME design
(@sec-analysis-plan-worked): a 25% event risk under usual care
against 20% under home health, at the evaluable sample size the
SAP (statistical analysis plan) computes for 80% power. Each task
gets its own random-number stream, derived from one seed, so that
tasks never share random numbers and any task can be rerun alone.

```{r}
#| label: cloud-sim-task
n_per_arm <- ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = 0.25, p2 = 0.20,
                                     power = 0.80)$n)

sim_task <- function(task_id, reps = 25, n = n_per_arm,
                     risks = c(0.25, 0.20), seed = 20260423) {
  old_kind <- RNGkind()[1]
  on.exit(RNGkind(old_kind))
  RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
  set.seed(seed)
  stream <- .Random.seed
  for (i in seq_len(task_id - 1)) {
    stream <- parallel::nextRNGStream(stream)
  }
  assign('.Random.seed', stream, envir = globalenv())
  p_value <- replicate(reps, {
    events <- rbinom(2, n, risks)
    prop.test(events, c(n, n))$p.value
  })
  data.frame(task = task_id, rep = seq_len(reps), p_value = p_value)
}
```

On the cluster, `sim_task.R` calls `sim_task()` with the index from
the command line and saves the result as `results/task-<index>.rds`.
Here the chunk runs eight tasks one after another, which is what the
array does in parallel:

```{r}
#| label: cloud-sim-run
results_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), 'results')
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
n_tasks <- 8
for (id in seq_len(n_tasks)) {
  saveRDS(sim_task(id),
          file.path(results_dir, sprintf('task-%03d.rds', id)))
}
list.files(results_dir)
```

The step that combines the tasks is where the opening's failure
happened, so it checks that every task it expects is present
before it reads any of them:

```{r}
#| label: cloud-sim-combine
library(purrr)

combine_tasks <- function(dir, n_tasks) {
  expected <- file.path(dir, sprintf('task-%03d.rds',
                                     seq_len(n_tasks)))
  missing <- basename(expected[!file.exists(expected)])
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop(length(missing), ' of ', n_tasks, ' tasks missing: ',
         paste(missing, collapse = ', '), call. = FALSE)
  }
  list_rbind(map(expected, readRDS))
}

sims <- combine_tasks(results_dir, n_tasks)
power_hat <- mean(sims$p_value < 0.05)
mc_se <- sqrt(power_hat * (1 - power_hat) / nrow(sims))
power_exact <- power.prop.test(n = n_per_arm, p1 = 0.25,
                              p2 = 0.20)$power
c(replicates = nrow(sims), power = power_hat, mc_se = mc_se)
```

The estimate from `r nrow(sims)` replicates is
`r round(power_hat, 3)`, with a Monte Carlo standard error of
`r round(mc_se, 3)`; the analytic power at this sample size is
`r sprintf('%.3f', power_exact)`. A real study runs enough
replicates to make the Monte Carlo standard error small against
the differences it reports, and states the replicate count it
actually achieved.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Combining whatever files exist turns a killed task into a
smaller study.** Delete one task's output, as an out-of-memory
kill would, and the convenient idiom still returns a plausible
estimate:

```{r}
#| label: cloud-sim-pitfall
#| error: true
file.remove(file.path(results_dir, 'task-003.rds'))
naive <- list_rbind(map(list.files(results_dir, full.names = TRUE),
                        readRDS))
c(replicates = nrow(naive), power = mean(naive$p_value < 0.05))
combine_tasks(results_dir, n_tasks)
```

`list.files()` found seven files and returned an estimate from
`r nrow(naive)` replicates as readily as from `r nrow(sims)`, without
a word; the guarded `combine_tasks()` names the missing task and
stops.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before summarizing a job array, confirm it from both sides: the
scheduler says every task completed, and the results directory
holds one file per task. On the cluster (display-only):

```bash
sacct -j <array-id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode -X \
  | grep -v COMPLETED
```

prints only the header when every task completed; any line below
it names a task that failed, timed out, or ran out of memory. In R,
`combine_tasks()` is the second check: it refuses to summarize an
incomplete set.
:::

Within one node, the parallelism is R's own. The `future`
framework [@bengtsson2021future] runs the same code sequentially
on a laptop and across a node's cores by changing one line, the
plan, which keeps the parallel and serial versions of an analysis
from diverging. A job array is the better tool when the tasks are
independent and many; `future` is the better tool inside a single
long task.

### Exercises

2. A colleague's batch script reads `#SBATCH --mem=500M` and
   `#SBATCH --output=out/%x_%j.out`, and `sacct` reports
   `OUT_OF_MEMORY` with `MaxRSS` of `499M`. A second attempt with
   `--mem=8G` fails at once and leaves no log. Explain both
   failures and fix the script.
3. Run `sim_task(3)` twice, with other random draws in between,
   and confirm that the two results are identical and differ from
   `sim_task(4)`. Why does that matter when a cluster task is
   killed?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
2. The first run used all the memory it requested and was killed
   at the limit. The second failed because SLURM does not create
   the `out/` directory named in `--output`, so the job could not
   open its log. Request memory with headroom (for example
   `--mem=1G`, a third or more above the observed peak, or more
   if the data will grow) and run `mkdir -p out` before `sbatch`.

3. Each task's random-number stream is derived from the seed and
   the task index alone, so the rerun matches exactly, whatever
   happened to the session's random numbers in between:

```{r}
#| label: soln-06-3
first_run <- sim_task(3)
invisible(runif(100))
rerun <- sim_task(3)
stopifnot(identical(first_run, rerun),
          !identical(rerun$p_value, sim_task(4)$p_value))
head(rerun, 3)
```

When a task is killed, you resubmit only that index
(`sbatch --array=3 sim.sbatch`) and get the replicates the full
run would have produced, instead of rerunning the whole study or
mixing streams.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does `sim_task()` derive a separate stream for
each task with `parallel::nextRNGStream()` instead of calling
`set.seed(20260423)` in every task?

**Answer.** With the same seed in every task, every task draws the
same random numbers, so 40 tasks of 25 replicates are 25
replicates repeated 40 times, and the Monte Carlo standard error
computed from 1,000 rows is far too small. The L'Ecuyer streams are
distinct by construction and depend only on the seed and the task
index, so the study is both correct and reproducible task by task.
:::

## Planning and reporting a simulation study {#sec-cloud-sim}

The job array of @sec-cloud-hpc ran a simulation already; this
section asks what the simulation should have been before any task
was submitted. A large simulation study is the textbook case for a
job array, because it is many independent, identical replicates,
but running thousands of replicates efficiently does not make the
study well designed. A simulation study answers a question about
the properties of a statistical method, and like any study it
needs a plan written before the data, here the pseudo-random
numbers, are generated.

### The ADEMP framework

Morris, White, and Crowther propose organizing a simulation
study's plan around five elements, memorably ordered as ADEMP
[@morris2019using]: **A**ims, the specific question the study
answers; **D**ata-generating mechanisms, the models used to
simulate data, with the scenarios (sample sizes, effect sizes,
correlation structures) varied across; **E**stimands, the
quantities the methods under study are trying to estimate;
**M**ethods, the estimators or procedures being compared; and
**P**erformance measures, the statistics that summarize how well
each method recovered the estimand across the simulated replicates
(bias, coverage, power, and so on). Writing the plan in this order,
before any code runs, catches a common failure mode: a simulation
coded first and described later tends to acquire scenarios and
measures that happened to be convenient to program, rather than the
ones the aims required.

For the job array of @sec-cloud-hpc, an ADEMP sketch might read:
the aim is to estimate the power of the two-proportion test at the
HF-HOME design's planned sample size; the data-generating mechanism
is independent binomial outcomes at the usual-care and home-health
risks under the alternative; the estimand is the test's rejection
probability; the method is `prop.test()`; and the performance
measure is the empirical rejection rate, which @sec-cloud-hpc
reported alongside its Monte Carlo standard error. The rest of this
section is about that last word: Monte Carlo standard error, the
piece of a simulation report that is easy to omit and that tells
the reader whether the simulation ran long enough to trust.

### Monte Carlo error on a performance measure

A simulation study estimates a performance measure, such as bias or
coverage, from a finite number of replicates, `r`'`nsim`'`, and like
any estimate from a finite sample, it has its own standard error:
the *Monte Carlo standard error* (MCSE). Reporting a performance
measure without its MCSE is like reporting a trial's risk
difference without a confidence interval; the reader cannot tell
whether 94 percent coverage, from 50 replicates, differs
meaningfully from the nominal 95 percent. Three measures and their
MCSEs appear in almost every simulation report, and each MCSE is a
function of a quantity the simulation already computed:

$$
\widehat{\text{bias}} = \bar{\hat\theta} - \theta, \qquad
\text{MCSE}(\widehat{\text{bias}}) = \frac{\widehat{SE}}{\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}}
$$

$$
\widehat{SE} = \text{sd}(\hat\theta), \qquad
\text{MCSE}(\widehat{SE}) = \frac{\widehat{SE}}{\sqrt{2(n_{\text{sim}} - 1)}}
$$

$$
\widehat{\text{coverage}} = \frac{1}{n_{\text{sim}}}
  \sum_i \mathbb{1}(\text{CI}_i \ni \theta), \qquad
\text{MCSE}(\widehat{\text{coverage}}) =
  \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\text{coverage}}(1 - \widehat{\text{coverage}})}
             {n_{\text{sim}}}}
$$

where $\theta$ is the true value of the estimand (known, because
the data were simulated) and $\hat\theta_i$ and $\text{CI}_i$ are
the estimate and confidence interval from replicate $i$. Each MCSE
shrinks with $\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}$, the same arithmetic as the
Monte Carlo standard error of a power estimate in @sec-cloud-hpc,
which is why a simulation study, like a job array, wants many
replicates: not for the point estimate alone, but to make its own
uncertainty small enough to be worth reporting.

### A worked example, by hand

The loop below is deliberately plain: base R, no package beyond
what every R installation ships, so that the mechanics of bias,
empirical SE, and coverage, and of their MCSEs, are visible rather
than hidden inside a function call. The scenario is a smaller-N
version of the HF-HOME design, usual care at a 25 percent 30-day
event risk against home health at 20 percent, so that it runs in a
fraction of a second rather than needing the job array:

```{r}
#| label: cloud-ademp-sim
n_per_arm_small <- 30
true_rd <- 0.25 - 0.20

sim_one_trial <- function(n = n_per_arm_small, p1 = 0.25, p2 = 0.20) {
  y1 <- rbinom(1, n, p1)
  y2 <- rbinom(1, n, p2)
  p1_hat <- y1 / n
  p2_hat <- y2 / n
  est <- p1_hat - p2_hat
  se <- sqrt(p1_hat * (1 - p1_hat) / n + p2_hat * (1 - p2_hat) / n)
  ci <- est + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
  c(est = est, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}

set.seed(20261011)
n_sim <- 2000
draws <- vapply(seq_len(n_sim), function(i) sim_one_trial(), double(3))
ests <- draws["est", ]
covered <- draws["lower", ] <= true_rd & draws["upper", ] >= true_rd

bias_hat <- mean(ests) - true_rd
emp_se <- sd(ests)
coverage_hat <- mean(covered)

mcse_bias <- emp_se / sqrt(n_sim)
mcse_se <- emp_se / sqrt(2 * (n_sim - 1))
mcse_coverage <- sqrt(coverage_hat * (1 - coverage_hat) / n_sim)

round(c(bias = bias_hat, mcse_bias = mcse_bias,
       emp_se = emp_se, mcse_emp_se = mcse_se,
       coverage = coverage_hat, mcse_coverage = mcse_coverage), 4)
```

From `r n_sim` replicates, the estimated bias is
`r sprintf('%.4f', bias_hat)` (Monte Carlo standard error
`r sprintf('%.4f', mcse_bias)`), consistent with an unbiased
estimator at this precision. Coverage is
`r sprintf('%.3f', coverage_hat)` (Monte Carlo standard error
`r sprintf('%.3f', mcse_coverage)`), which should sit close to the
nominal 0.95 for a confidence interval built from the normal
approximation at this sample size; a value several MCSEs away from
0.95 would be evidence of a real problem with the method, not
simulation noise. Each line of the loop is one simulated trial, in
the Data-generating mechanism's terms; the vector of estimates and
coverage indicators across replicates is what the Performance
measures are computed from.

A real methods paper runs this scenario, and several others
varying the sample size and the event risks, at thousands of
replicates rather than a few hundred, which is exactly where
@sec-cloud-hpc's job array becomes the right tool: each scenario,
or each block of replicates within a scenario, is an independent
task, submitted the same way `sim_task()` was, and `combine_tasks()`
guards the combination step the same way. The MCSE formulas above
do not change when the replicates come from forty cluster tasks
instead of one `for` loop; what changes is how fast `n_sim` can grow
large enough to make the MCSEs small.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before trusting a simulation's MCSEs, confirm that the replicates
behind them are actually independent, the assumption every formula
above relies on. If the simulation runs on a job array, that means
the same check as @sec-cloud-hpc: one random-number stream per
task, derived from the seed and the task index, never the same
seed repeated across tasks. A simulation whose scenarios share a
random-number stream understates its own MCSEs, exactly as a
coverage estimate from repeated replicates would, and the formulas
give a false sense of precision.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague reports '94.6 percent coverage' for a new
method from 100 simulated trials, with no Monte Carlo standard
error. Is 94.6 percent meaningfully below the nominal 95 percent?

**Answer.** Not necessarily, and the report cannot say either way
without the MCSE. With `coverage_hat = 0.946` and `n_sim = 100`,
$\text{MCSE} = \sqrt{0.946 \times 0.054 / 100} \approx 0.023$, so the
observed coverage is well within one MCSE of 0.95. The gap looks
meaningful only because the report omitted the number that would
have shown it was not. More replicates, not a different method,
would be the first thing to ask for.
:::

### Exercises

1. Using `sim_one_trial()` above, increase `n_sim` to 10,000 and
   recompute the three MCSEs. By roughly what factor should each
   shrink relative to the `n_sim = 2000` run, and does the result
   match the $\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}$ arithmetic?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Each MCSE is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}$, so
increasing `n_sim` by a factor of 5 should shrink each MCSE by a
factor of about $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$:

```{r}
#| label: soln-06-ademp-1
set.seed(20261011)
n_sim_big <- 10000
draws_big <- vapply(seq_len(n_sim_big), function(i) sim_one_trial(),
                    double(3))
emp_se_big <- sd(draws_big["est", ])
c(ratio_expected = sqrt(n_sim_big / n_sim),
  ratio_observed = (emp_se_big / sqrt(n_sim_big)) / mcse_bias)
```

The observed ratio is close to the expected $\sqrt{5}$, with the
small discrepancy coming from Monte Carlo noise in `emp_se_big`
itself, which has its own MCSE.
:::

## Working on a remote machine {#sec-cloud-remote}

Whether the machine is a cluster login node or a cloud instance,
two everyday problems are the same: keeping a job alive after you
disconnect, and moving data to and from the machine.

### Keeping a job alive

You SSH in, start a job, and your laptop goes to sleep or the
wireless connection drops. The job dies with your shell, and whatever
it had computed dies with it. The mechanism explains why each
remedy works: when the connection closes, the shell receives a
hangup signal, `SIGHUP`, and relays it to the processes it
started, whose default response is to terminate. Each remedy
either keeps the process from receiving the signal or gives it a
parent other than the shell you are about to lose.

| Remedy | How the job survives | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `nohup` | The command ignores `SIGHUP`; output goes to a file | A single script you start and check later |
| `tmux` (or the older `screen`) | The job runs in a session that outlives the connection | You want to reattach and watch, or work interactively |
| `systemd` service | The system, not your shell, runs it | Something that runs on a schedule, in production |
| `sbatch` | The scheduler runs it on a compute node | Any work on a cluster |

: Ways to keep a remote job alive. {#tbl-cloud-detach}

The first two, display-only:

```bash
nohup Rscript analysis.R > analysis.log 2>&1 &
tail -f analysis.log                 # watch; Ctrl-C stops watching only

tmux new -s analysis                 # start a named session
Rscript analysis.R                   # inside tmux
# detach with Ctrl-b d, log out, and later:
tmux attach -t analysis
```

### Moving data

To copy a file or a directory to the machine (display-only):

```bash
scp -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem data.csv ubuntu@<ip>:/home/ubuntu/data/
rsync -avz -e "ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem" \
  ./data/ ubuntu@<ip>:/home/ubuntu/data/
```

`rsync` transfers only changed files, which helps when iterating.
For larger or longer-term storage on AWS, the object store S3
(@sec-cloud-aws) is cheaper than the instance's own disk:

```bash
aws s3 cp results.rds s3://my-bucket/project/results.rds
aws s3 sync ./output s3://my-bucket/project/output/
```

Data leaving a cloud provider (egress) is charged and data
arriving is free, so plan large downloads; @tbl-cloud-as-of gives
the rate.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
After a transfer, compare checksums at both ends rather than file
sizes (display-only):

```bash
shasum -a 256 data/visits.csv                        # on the laptop
ssh ubuntu@<ip> sha256sum /home/ubuntu/data/visits.csv
```

The two hashes must match. A truncated transfer can leave a file
that reads without error and is missing its last rows.
:::

### Exercises

4. You start `Rscript analysis.R &` (without `nohup`) on a remote
   server, and your wireless connection drops. You reconnect an
   hour later. `ps aux | grep
   analysis` shows nothing and `analysis.log` does not exist. What
   happened, and which two changes would have prevented it?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The trailing `&` puts the job in the background of your shell but
leaves it one of that shell's jobs. When the connection dropped,
the shell received the hangup and relayed it to its jobs, which
terminated the analysis. There is no log because the command
never redirected its output to a file. Either `nohup Rscript analysis.R >
analysis.log 2>&1 &`, which ignores the hangup and writes a log, or
starting the job inside `tmux` would have kept it alive; on a
cluster, `sbatch` replaces both.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You SSH into a cloud instance, start a long analysis
with `Rscript analysis.R`, and close your laptop. What happens to
the analysis?

**Answer.** When the connection drops, the process receives a
hangup signal and terminates, and the partial results are gone.
`nohup`, `tmux`, a `systemd` service, or a scheduler would each
have kept it running (@tbl-cloud-detach). Forgetting this is the
classic 'I let it run overnight and it died' surprise.
:::

## The public cloud, minimally {#sec-cloud-aws}

When the cluster is unavailable, its queue is too slow, or the job
needs hardware it lacks, you rent. The dominant providers overlap
heavily, and this chapter uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) for
concreteness:

| Provider | Note |
|---|---|
| AWS | The largest catalog; the examples below |
| Google Cloud Platform (GCP) | Comparable services under different names |
| Microsoft Azure | Convenient where the institution already uses Microsoft accounts |
| Smaller providers (DigitalOcean, Linode) | Simpler and cheaper for small work; fewer features |
| University HPC cluster | Usually free; queued; no Docker (@sec-cloud-hpc) |

: Where to run a job that has outgrown the laptop. For most
academic work the order is laptop, university cluster, public
cloud. {#tbl-cloud-providers}

### Before you provision anything: a budget and an alert

A cloud account bills from the first minute, and nothing in it
stops by default. The first step, before any instance exists, is
a budget that emails you when spending crosses a threshold. In the
console this is Billing, then Budgets; from the command line, with
two small files describing the budget and the alert
(display-only):

```json
{
  "BudgetName": "practicum-monthly",
  "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "25", "Unit": "USD"},
  "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
  "BudgetType": "COST"
}
```

```json
[
  {
    "Notification": {
      "NotificationType": "ACTUAL",
      "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
      "Threshold": 50,
      "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"
    },
    "Subscribers": [
      {"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "you@example.edu"}
    ]
  }
]
```

```bash
aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id "$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account \
                  --output text)" \
  --budget file://budget.json \
  --notifications-with-subscribers file://notify.json
```

A budget alerts; it does not stop anything, and billing data reach
it hours after the spending. The stopping mechanisms are the
idle alarm and the job script in @sec-cloud-cost.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
List the account's budgets and confirm yours, with its limit
(display-only):

```bash
aws budgets describe-budgets \
  --account-id "$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account \
                  --output text)" \
  --query 'Budgets[].[BudgetName,BudgetLimit.Amount]' --output table
```

Then confirm the subscription email arrived and that you accepted
it; an alert sent to an unconfirmed address reaches no one.
:::

### The services you need

The AWS catalog has hundreds of services; a biostatistician needs
about six.

| Term | What it is | What to know |
|---|---|---|
| EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) | Virtual machines, called instances | Billed per second of running time, whatever the machine is doing |
| Instance type | The machine size, such as `c6i.4xlarge` | The family letter signals the balance: `c` compute, `r` memory, `t` small burstable, `g` GPU |
| AMI (Amazon Machine Image) | The operating-system image an instance boots from | IDs differ by region and change often; look them up, never hard-code them |
| EBS (Elastic Block Store) | The instance's disk | Persists when the instance is stopped; deleted when it is terminated |
| S3 (Simple Storage Service) | Object storage for files | Cheaper than EBS for data the analysis has finished with |
| IAM (Identity and Access Management) | Users, roles, and permissions | Give machines roles, people single sign-on, and nobody long-lived keys |
| Security group | A firewall around an instance | Allow SSH (port 22) from your own address only |
| Spot instance | Spare capacity at a discount | AWS can reclaim it with two minutes' notice |

: AWS in one table. Prices and current instance types are in
@tbl-cloud-as-of. {#tbl-cloud-glossary}

### Credentials: single sign-on and instance roles

Sign in through IAM Identity Center (single sign-on, SSO, which an
institutional account usually provides) and let the AWS command
line interface (CLI) fetch short-lived credentials. Give an
instance the permissions it needs, to write to one S3 bucket, say,
through an IAM role attached to the instance, never by copying
access keys onto it. Long-lived access keys for an IAM user are
the credential most often leaked, in a committed file or a pasted
log, and the hardest to notice once leaked.

Install version 2 of the CLI and configure it once (display-only):

```bash
brew install awscli                  # macOS (Homebrew ships v2)
# Linux (x86_64): AWS's official installer; Windows has an MSI
curl -fsSL "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" \
  -o awscliv2.zip
unzip awscliv2.zip && sudo ./aws/install

aws configure sso                    # short-lived SSO credentials
aws ec2 describe-instances --query \
  'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name]' \
  --output table
```

Avoid `pip install awscli`, which many older tutorials show: the
`awscli` package on PyPI is still version 1 of the CLI, which
lacks `aws configure sso` among other things. The browser console
is good for learning and one-off inspection; the CLI is what makes
a job scripted and repeatable.

### Launching an instance

Launch from the CLI (display-only). The `resolve:ssm:` form looks
up the parameter Canonical publishes in AWS Systems Manager (SSM)
for the current Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (long-term support) image in
whatever region you are using, so the command does not go stale:

```bash
AMI=resolve:ssm:/aws/service/canonical/ubuntu/server/\
24.04/stable/current/amd64/hvm/ebs-gp3/ami-id

aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id "$AMI" \
  --instance-type t3.large \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abcd1234 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abcd1234 \
  --tag-specifications \
    'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Project,Value=hfhome}]'
```

A literal AMI ID such as `ami-0c7217cdde317cfec` names one image in
one region, and Ubuntu publishes a new one every few weeks, so a
hard-coded ID is wrong in every other region and stale within a
month. To see the ID the parameter resolves to, pass the path
after `resolve:ssm:` to `aws ssm get-parameter --name <path>
--query Parameter.Value`.

Connect, and run the project's container rather than installing R
by hand (display-only). A fresh Ubuntu instance does not have
Docker, so install it first (Ubuntu's `docker.io` package, or
Docker's own apt repository for a current release):

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-keypair.pem ubuntu@<public-ip>

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y docker.io git
sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu       # log out and back in once
git clone https://github.com/you/project.git && cd project
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/work my-analysis-image:v1.0 \
  Rscript /work/analysis/scripts/main.R
```

The container is what makes the instance reproducible: a cloud
machine needs the same environment specification as the laptop
that ran the analysis, and the image of @sec-docker is that
specification. Installing `r-base` from apt and running
`renv::restore()` also works, but it gives you the R version
Ubuntu packages, not the one your lockfile records.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm what you launched and that it is tagged, so that you can
find it again (display-only):

```bash
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters 'Name=tag:Project,Values=hfhome' \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,State.Name]' \
  --output table
```

Every instance you started should appear, with the type you
intended. An instance you cannot find by tag is one you will
forget to stop.
:::

### Where the data may go

Provisioning is a form to fill in. Deciding what data may sit on
the machine is where the compliance exposure lives. Protected
health information (PHI) on a personal AWS account is a violation
in most institutions. Use the institutional account, keep data
inside the institutional network where the account provides for
it, and treat 'I'll just upload the CSV to my personal bucket for
testing' as a red flag.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Your simulation study is too slow on a laptop, so you
plan to move it to EC2. The data are de-identified under Safe
Harbor. Is that sufficient to proceed?

**Answer.** No. De-identification answers one of three separate
questions, and the other two are the ones that stop projects.

The first is contractual. A data use agreement (DUA) typically
names where data may be stored and processed, and many prohibit
third-party cloud entirely or require specific arrangements. Safe
Harbor de-identification does not release you from a DUA you
signed, and an institutional review board (IRB) protocol naming
institutional servers is a commitment you cannot vary alone.

The second is regulatory. Under HIPAA (the Health Insurance
Portability and Accountability Act), using a cloud provider for PHI
requires a Business Associate Agreement (BAA). Your institution may
hold one covering specific AWS accounts under specific
configurations; the personal account you opened with a credit card
is not covered by it.

The third is the one @sec-deident already made: Safe Harbor
produces data that are de-identified, not anonymous. Residual
re-identification risk is why the DUA and the BAA exist at all.

The practical order is: read the DUA, ask whether your institution
has a covered account, and only then compare instance prices. A
simulation study on synthetic data raises none of this, which is
often the cheapest way through.
:::

## Cost and failure handling {#sec-cloud-cost}

Cloud billing surprises share a structure. The meter runs on
elapsed time rather than on work done, so an idle instance costs
exactly what a busy one costs, and nothing in the system produces
an event when your analysis finishes. A laptop that has finished
its job sits there quietly; a rented machine that has finished its
job sits there quietly and bills you for it, over a weekend, from a
browser tab you closed on Friday. Every practice in this section
supplies the stopping event the platform does not.

### What it costs

Prices, instance types, and image paths are the most perishable
facts in this book, so they live in one dated table, and every
cost quoted in this chapter is computed from it.

```{r}
#| label: cloud-as-of-data
#| include: false
aws_as_of <- data.frame(
  item = c('t3.large', 'c6i.xlarge', 'c6i.4xlarge', 'r6i.4xlarge',
           'g4dn.12xlarge', 'S3 Standard storage',
           'EBS gp3 volume', 'Data transfer out to the internet'),
  spec = c('2 vCPU, 8 GiB', '4 vCPU, 8 GiB', '16 vCPU, 32 GiB',
           '16 vCPU, 128 GiB', '48 vCPU, 192 GiB, 4 GPUs',
           'Object storage, first 50 TB a month',
           'General-purpose solid-state disk',
           'First 10 TB a month, after 100 GB free'),
  usd = c(0.0832, 0.17, 0.68, 1.008, 3.912, 0.023, 0.08, 0.09),
  unit = c(rep('hour', 5), 'GB-month', 'GB-month', 'GB'),
  checked = as.Date('2026-10-10')
)
price <- function(x) aws_as_of$usd[aws_as_of$item == x]
hours_per_month <- 730
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cloud-as-of
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "AWS facts this chapter relies on: on-demand Linux
#|   prices in the us-east-1 region. Every price was checked on the
#|   date shown against AWS's published price-list data; none is an
#|   estimate. The 100 GB of free transfer out is pooled across
#|   services and regions each month. Prices change and differ
#|   by region; check the AWS pricing pages before you budget. Spot
#|   capacity is advertised at up to 90 percent below on-demand, and
#|   the actual discount varies by type, region, and week. Free-tier
#|   eligibility also changes: check the console for eligible types
#|   (`t3.medium` is not among them). Ubuntu 24.04 images: the SSM
#|   path in the launch example, not a literal AMI ID."
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Item = aws_as_of$item, Specification = aws_as_of$spec,
             `Price (USD)` = sprintf('%.4g per %s', aws_as_of$usd,
                                     aws_as_of$unit),
             Checked = format(aws_as_of$checked),
             check.names = FALSE)
)
```

vCPU is a virtual CPU (central processing unit), usually one
hardware thread, so 16 vCPU is typically 8 physical cores. GiB is a
gibibyte, 2^30^ bytes. At these rates a `g4dn.12xlarge` left
running for a week costs
\$`r format(round(price('g4dn.12xlarge') * 24 * 7), big.mark = ',')`,
more than a small laptop.

### Spot instances

Spot instances are spare capacity sold at a steep discount, and the
catch is that AWS can reclaim them with two minutes' notice. For
embarrassingly parallel simulations that save their results as
they go, spot is usually the cheapest option available, provided
the job can resume from its last saved state: the job array of
@sec-cloud-hpc, writing one file per task, has exactly this
property (display-only):

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances --instance-type c6i.xlarge \
  --instance-market-options 'MarketType=spot' \
  ...
```

### A job script that always stops the instance

End every job by uploading its results and shutting the instance
down, and configure the instance to *stop* (not terminate) on
shutdown; a stopped instance bills only for its disk. The upload
and shutdown must happen whether the analysis succeeded or failed
(display-only):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-job.sh: upload and shut down even if the analysis fails
set -euo pipefail

finish() {
  aws s3 cp analysis.log s3://my-bucket/project/ || true
  aws s3 cp results/ s3://my-bucket/project/results/ --recursive || true
  sudo shutdown -h now
}
trap finish EXIT

Rscript analysis.R > analysis.log 2>&1
```

The `#!` line must be the first line of the file, or it is an
ordinary comment. `set -e` stops the script at the first failing
command, and without the `trap` that would mean stopping before the
upload and the shutdown. The `trap` runs `finish` whenever the
script exits, so an error in `analysis.R` no longer leaves an idle
instance billing over the weekend, and the log reaches S3 either
way, which is where you will look first.

A second, independent stop is an alarm on the instance itself,
which stops it after an hour below 5% CPU use, whatever the script
did (display-only):

```bash
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "idle-stop-$INSTANCE_ID" \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value="$INSTANCE_ID" \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 12 \
  --threshold 5 --comparison-operator LessThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions "arn:aws:automate:$(aws configure get region):ec2:stop"
```

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft the job script, and test its failure path
yourself.

> **Context.** I run `Rscript analysis.R` on an EC2 instance
> launched with `--instance-initiated-shutdown-behavior stop` and an
> instance profile that may write to `s3://my-bucket/project/`. The
> script writes `results/` and a log.
>
> **Constraints.** Bash with `set -euo pipefail`; the `#!` line
> first. Use the instance role; never read, write, or ask me for
> access keys. Do not hard-code an AMI ID, a price, or a region.
> Do not launch, terminate, or modify any resource other than this
> instance's own shutdown.
>
> **Criteria.** Whether `analysis.R` succeeds or fails, the log and
> any results reach S3 and the instance shuts down. List every
> command that could fail and what happens to the upload and the
> shutdown if it does.

*Failure mode.* Drafts commonly put the upload and `shutdown`
after the `Rscript` line, where `set -e` skips them on the first
error, so a failed analysis leaves a running instance and no log.
Prices, AMI IDs, and instance types in a model's answer come from
its training data and are stale by construction; take them from
@tbl-cloud-as-of and the SSM path. *Check.* Add `quit(status = 1)`
as the first line of `analysis.R`, run the script, and confirm
that the instance reaches `stopped` and that the log is in S3. Put
the budget alert in place before any agent or script provisions
anything, and never paste keys into a prompt (@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Test the failure path, not only the success path. With the
deliberate failure in place (display-only):

```bash
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].State.Name' --output text
aws s3 ls s3://my-bucket/project/analysis.log
```

The first should print `stopped` within a few minutes; the second
should list the log, whose last lines show the R error.
:::

### The environmental cost of compute

A rented instance has a cost beyond the invoice: the electricity
it draws, and the carbon associated with generating that
electricity, which varies by region and by the data center's
energy mix. This book will not quote a figure for grams of
carbon dioxide per core-hour, because the honest number depends on
which grid supplies the data center, how the provider's published
efficiency claims are audited, and how quickly both change; any
specific emissions factor stated here would be stale, and possibly
wrong, before the ink dried. What does not need a number to be
true is the direction of the effect: a job that runs sixteen times
longer than it needs to, because nobody profiled it first
(@sec-cloud-shortage), or an idle instance billing over a weekend
(@sec-cloud-cost), draws power for no analytical benefit, and that
is a cost in more than money. Treat job efficiency, the same habit
that keeps a budget under control, as an environmental
consideration as well as a financial one: profile before you
scale, choose the smallest instance that finishes the job, and
shut the machine down the moment it is done. A researcher who
wants a defensible number for a specific provider and region
should consult that provider's own published sustainability
reporting rather than a general estimate, and should expect the
reporting itself to be contested.

### Exercises

5. Using @tbl-cloud-as-of, what does a `c6i.xlarge` cost if it runs
   a 3-hour job and is then forgotten, running idle, until Monday
   morning 60 hours later? What would the job script above have
   cost instead, ignoring the disk?
6. A job script ends with the two lines `Rscript analysis.R >
   analysis.log 2>&1` and `sudo shutdown -h now`, and begins with
   `set -euo pipefail`. What happens when `analysis.R` fails?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
5. The forgotten instance runs 63 hours:

```{r}
#| label: soln-06-5
forgotten <- price('c6i.xlarge') * (3 + 60)
scripted <- price('c6i.xlarge') * 3
round(c(forgotten = forgotten, scripted = scripted), 2)
```

The idle weekend costs
`r round(forgotten / scripted)` times the job itself. The number
is small for this instance and large for the GPU types in the same
table; the habit is the same.

6. `Rscript` exits with a non-zero status, `set -e` stops the
   script, and `shutdown` never runs: the instance keeps billing
   and the only log is on its disk. The `trap ... EXIT` form runs
   the upload and the shutdown on every exit path.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You set a monthly budget of \$25 with an alert at 50
percent. Does it protect you from a `g4dn.12xlarge` left running
over a weekend?

**Answer.** It tells you, late; it does not stop anything. Budget
data lag spending by hours, and the alert is an email. At the rate
in @tbl-cloud-as-of the instance passes \$12.50 within a few hours
of launch and keeps billing until someone acts. The stop has to
come from the job script's `trap`, the idle alarm, or both; the
budget is the backstop that tells you one of them failed.
:::

## Worked example: the simulation on AWS {#sec-cloud-worked}

The job array of @sec-cloud-hpc, run instead on one cloud
instance because the cluster queue is days long. The whole
sequence is display-only.

```bash
# 0. the budget alert exists (see above)

# 1. provision ($AMI as set in the launch example)
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id "$AMI" \
  --instance-type c6i.4xlarge \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abcd1234 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abcd1234 \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=sim-s3-writer \
  --instance-initiated-shutdown-behavior stop \
  --user-data file://bootstrap.sh \
  --tag-specifications \
    'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Project,Value=sim2026}]'

# bootstrap.sh installs Docker, clones the repository, runs the
# simulation in the project image, uploads results to S3, and
# shuts down (with a trap, as above); the instance profile lets it
# write to S3 without access keys

# 2. wait for it to finish (and shut down)
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids <id> \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].State.Name'

# 3. retrieve results
aws s3 cp s3://my-bucket/sim2026/results/ results/ --recursive

# 4. terminate the instance (delete it and its disk for good)
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids <id>
```

```{r}
#| label: cloud-worked-cost
#| include: false
run_hours <- 4
disk_gb <- 30
compute_cost <- price('c6i.4xlarge') * run_hours
disk_cost <- price('EBS gp3 volume') * disk_gb * run_hours /
  hours_per_month
laptop_hours <- 32
```

The cost, from @tbl-cloud-as-of: a `r run_hours`-hour run on a
`c6i.4xlarge` is \$`r sprintf('%.2f', compute_cost)`. A
`r disk_gb` GB disk for those hours is
\$`r sprintf('%.3f', disk_cost)`, although a stopped instance keeps
billing for its disk until step 4 terminates it. Downloading the
results costs pennies.

Suppose the same simulation took `r laptop_hours` hours on a
laptop. The cloud run cuts the wall-clock time by a factor of
`r laptop_hours / run_hours` for about \$`r round(compute_cost)`,
and the judgment is whether the time saved is worth it. Read that
factor as an observation about this one job, not as a rate to
expect: the 16 vCPU of a `c6i.4xlarge` are 8 physical cores, a
recent laptop has several cores of its own, and the serial part of
the job keeps the gain below the ratio of core counts. Time a short
pilot on both machines before deciding.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before you report anything from the cloud run, apply the checks
that would have caught the opening's failure: the results
directory holds one file per task, `combine_tasks()` runs without
error, and the replicate count in the methods section is
`nrow()` of what it returned. Then confirm that nothing is still
billing:

```bash
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters 'Name=tag:Project,Values=sim2026' \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].State.Name' --output text
```

It should print `terminated` or nothing at all.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 8: a missing task produces a plausible number.** Before
   summarizing a job array, confirm from the scheduler and from
   the files that every task completed, and report the replicate
   count you achieved.
2. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** Run remote jobs in the
   project's image (Apptainer on a cluster, Docker on a cloud
   instance), not in whatever R the machine happens to have.
3. **Habit 12: every model output is a hypothesis until
   verified.** Prices, AMI IDs, and scripts from a model are
   checked against the dated table and a deliberate failure, and
   a model never sees your keys.

## Cumulative practice

7. *Cumulative (uses @sec-docker and @sec-analysis-plan).* Package
   `sim_task()` and `combine_tasks()` from this chapter as
   `analysis/scripts/sim_task.R` in a project with the canonical
   Dockerfile (@sec-docker-canonical). Write the job-array script
   for 40 tasks of 25 replicates, and, if you have cluster access,
   run it. Whether or not you run it, write the two checks you
   would make before reporting the power estimate, and the
   sentence of the methods section that reports the replicate
   count and the Monte Carlo standard error.
8. *On your own work (no key).* Take a long-running analysis of
   yours, name its shortage using @tbl-cloud-shortages, estimate
   its cost on the cheapest suitable tier from @tbl-cloud-as-of or
   your cluster's documentation, and run it there with a budget
   alert (if in the cloud) and a script that stops the machine on
   every exit path. Record the cost and the wall-clock time.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
7. The two checks are the two sides of the job-array Verification:
   `sacct ... -X | grep -v COMPLETED` prints only its header, and
   `combine_tasks(results_dir, 40)` returns 1,000 rows without
   error. The methods sentence states the achieved count and the
   precision, computed rather than typed, for example:

   ```qmd
   Power was estimated from `{{r}} nrow(sims)` simulated trials
   (Monte Carlo standard error `{{r}} round(mc_se, 3)`).
   ```

   The script should create `logs/` and `results/` before
   `sbatch`, request memory with headroom over a measured peak,
   and derive each task's random-number stream from the seed and
   the task index.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Submit a batch job | `sbatch job.sbatch` | Computing on the login node |
| Submit a job array | `#SBATCH --array=1-40%10` | Hand-launching many jobs |
| See how jobs ended | `sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,ReqMem` | Out-of-memory and timeout kills going unnoticed |
| Run a container on a cluster | `apptainer exec analysis.sif Rscript ...` | A different R on the cluster |
| Refuse an incomplete array | `combine_tasks(dir, n_tasks)` | Summarizing a smaller study than planned |
| Survive a disconnect | `nohup ... &` or `tmux new -s name` | `SIGHUP` killing the job |
| Copy or sync data | `rsync -avz`, `aws s3 sync` | Re-sending unchanged files |
| Set a budget alert | `aws budgets create-budget` | Discovering the bill a month later |
| Get credentials | `aws configure sso` | Long-lived keys that leak |
| Look up the current Ubuntu image | `resolve:ssm:/aws/service/canonical/...` | Stale or wrong-region AMI IDs |
| Always upload and stop | `trap finish EXIT` | An idle instance after a failure |
| Stop an idle instance | `aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm ... ec2:stop` | A script that never ran its trap |

: Remote compute at a glance. {#tbl-cloud-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-06}

1. Remote compute supplies a resource the laptop has run out of:
   cores for parallel work, memory for a job that cannot run at
   all on the laptop, or simply a machine that is not your own,
   so the laptop stays free. A simulation that takes 10 hours on
   one laptop core might take between 1.25 hours (the eightfold
   ideal, never quite reached) and 2 hours on an 8-core machine.
   For academic work, a university cluster is usually the first
   choice and the public cloud the second. The trade-offs are
   cost, data governance, and transfer overhead.
2. The AWS Management Console is a browser interface, good for
   learning the platform, one-off launches, and inspecting state.
   The AWS CLI (command line interface) is a command-line tool,
   essential for automation, scripting, and repeatable setup. Most
   professional workflows use the CLI for routine work and the
   console for inspection and debugging.
3. Use `nohup Rscript analysis.R > analysis.log 2>&1 &` to make
   the process ignore the hangup signal sent at logout, or run it
   inside a `tmux` or `screen` session that persists after logout;
   on a cluster, submit it with `sbatch`. Reconnect later with
   `tail -f analysis.log` or `tmux attach`. Without one of these,
   closing your shell kills the job.
